issues.legal_issue: A law abolishing enforceable cash grants cannot use the State’s acquisition power to appropriate money or choses in action for the purpose of increasing State revenue.
material_facts: The respondents held rights to receive cash grants enforceable against the State.
The challenged enactment discontinued the grants and provided for compensation to the grantees.
The State’s abolition of the grants would relieve it of its payment liability and augment its resources.
issues.conclusion: The enactment was invalid under Article 31(2), which does not permit the acquisition of money or choses in action to enrich the State’s coffers; compensation under that Article must be the just equivalent of the property taken.
issues.legal_principle: Article 31(2), construed harmoniously with Article 19(1)(f), does not authorize acquisition of money or choses in action for the purpose of raising State revenue, and requires compensation to be the just equivalent of the property taken. The Court followed State of Bihar v. Kameshwar Singh and Bombay Dyeing and Manufacturing Co. Ltd. v. State of Bombay.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_grant_abolit: A person challenged the validity of a law that abolishes cash grants.
predicates.enforceable_money_rights_extinguished: The law extinguished rights to receive money that were enforceable against the State.
predicates.state_revenue_is_the_purpose: The State used the abolition to increase its resources or revenue.

issues.definition: If a challenged grant-abolition law extinguishes enforceable rights to State payments in order to increase State revenue, the law is unconstitutional.

issues.legal_issue: A law depriving a person of property solely to increase State resources is not a reasonable restriction in the interest of the general public.
material_facts: The enactment extinguished the grantees’ rights to receive money from the State.
The enactment enabled the State to retain resources by ending its liability to pay the grants.
The State relied on the law as authority for depriving the grantees of their property.
issues.conclusion: The enactment was also invalid under Article 19(1)(f), because the restriction was not saved by Article 19(5).
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 31(1), a law authorizing deprivation of property must be valid and satisfy Article 19(1)(f), including the requirement in Article 19(5) that a restriction be reasonable and in the interest of the general public. A law permitting the State to appropriate property solely to augment its resources does not meet that requirement. The Court relied on Kavalappara Kottarathil Kochuni v. State of Madras, State of Bihar v. Kameshwar Singh, and Bombay Dyeing and Manufacturing Co. Ltd. v. State of Bombay.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_property_dep: A person challenged a law authorizing the State to deprive that person of property.
predicates.state_appropriates_property: The law allows the State to take or retain property belonging to another person.
predicates.state_revenue_is_the_purpose: The State uses the deprivation solely to increase its resources or revenue.

issues.definition: If a challenged law allows the State to appropriate another person’s property solely to increase State revenue, the law is unconstitutional.

issues.legal_issue: A statutory definition that covers distinct kinds of grants without a basis for separating valid from invalid applications cannot be upheld in part by severing some of those applications.
material_facts: The enactment defined cash grants broadly to include grants of different kinds, including grants in lieu of property or loans.
The definition did not distinguish among those kinds of grants.
The Court found no basis for separating some grants covered by the definition from others.
issues.conclusion: The definition had to stand or fall as a whole; because it was unconstitutional, the entire definition and the Act fell.
issues.legal_principle: The doctrine of severability permits separation only where the legal and unconstitutional parts of a provision can be separated; a court cannot rewrite an indivisible definition to limit it to applications the legislature might validly have enacted. The Court relied on Kameshwar Prasad v. State of Bihar.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_grant_defini: A person challenged the validity of a statutory definition of grants.
predicates.definition_covers_distinct_grant_types: The definition includes different kinds of grants without distinguishing among them.
predicates.no_separable_valid_part: The valid and invalid applications of the definition cannot be separated without rewriting it.

issues.definition: If a challenged definition covers distinct grant types and has no separable valid part, the entire definition is invalid.
